tour.title: Library, Terraces & the Great Theatre
tour.summary: Downhill through the best-preserved Roman city in the Aegean — council hall, temples, rich men's houses, the Celsus library and a theatre that held twenty-five thousand.
tour.overviewText:
You are about to walk down a Roman street that has been in continuous use, in one form or another, for more than two thousand years. The marble under your shoes is original. The ruts in it were cut by cart wheels before anyone alive was born, and the emperors whose statues lined this slope would still recognise the gradient, if nothing else.

Ephesus began as a Greek harbour town gathered around the sanctuary of Artemis — the goddess the Romans called Diana — whose temple here grew so vast the Greeks counted it among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. When Rome absorbed the Aegean coast, Ephesus became the capital of the rich province of Asia, and at its peak some two hundred thousand people lived here: sailors, bankers, priests, gladiators, and, famously, the apostle Paul, whose preaching against idols started a riot of silversmiths in the theatre you will stand in. The apostle John is traditionally said to have spent his last years here, and in 431 the Christian church held one of its great ecumenical councils in this city. Then the harbour silted up — the little Cayster river kept dumping mud where the ships needed depth — and Ephesus slowly choked: trade moved, malaria settled over the marshes, and the population drifted to the hill where the town of Selçuk stands today. Austrian archaeologists have been digging here since 1895, and they estimate barely a fifth of the ancient city is uncovered.

The walk itself is simple and downhill. You enter at the upper gate, follow the marble streets down through council halls, temples and rich men's houses, and come out at the lower gate by the harbour road — about a kilometre and a half on foot, all descending. What you are walking is the ancient city's own main street, in the order a Roman would have known it.

Practicals, plainly. The site opens at 08:00 in summer (to 19:00) — be at the upper gate at opening, because by ten the cruise buses arrive and the marble reflects the heat back at you. The site ticket is €40 and the Terrace Houses cost €15 more on top; pay in lira or by card, since euro cash is not accepted, and treat every figure as verify-at-the-gate. There is almost no shade, the marble is treacherously slippery when wet, and you want water, a hat, and shoes with grip. Start at the top: the whole route is designed to be walked downhill.

Go early, walk slowly, and touch the ruts in the marble. Somebody's cart made them.
tour.difficulty: Easy and all downhill, but the footing is the challenge: original marble slabs, polished by two millennia of feet, uneven and slippery when wet. Wear shoes with grip. Wheelchair users will struggle — there are steps and steep polished stretches throughout.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: At the 08:00 opening, starting at the upper gate so the whole walk descends ahead of the heat and the cruise-bus crowds. In summer 2026 the site also opens for night visits (to 23:00) on Wednesdays through Saturdays — a completely different, floodlit Ephesus — but the Terrace Houses close at 18:30 regardless, so do those first if you come late.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: Magnesia Gate (Upper Entrance)
stops.narration:
Start at the top, because the Romans built this city on a slope and every sensible visitor walks it downhill. This is the Magnesia Gate — the upper entrance, named for the road that once ran to the city of Magnesia — and the walls running off in both directions are Hellenistic, raised under Lysimachus, one of Alexander the Great's generals, when he refounded Ephesus here around 290 BC. Lysimachus moved the whole population to this spot by force, flooding the old town so people would relocate — ancient urban planning at its most direct.

Buy your ticket here: €40 for the site in 2026, pay in lira or by card, euro cash not accepted — verify at the gate, since the ministry revises prices. From this gate the marble street drops away below you all the way to the harbour plain, and that downhill line is your whole walk. Everything from here to the lower gate is inside one ticket.

One thing to understand before you descend: you are entering the fourth-largest city of the Roman Empire. Rome, Alexandria, Antioch — and Ephesus, capital of Asia, the province that covered most of western Turkey. Two hundred thousand people, the biggest harbour on this coast, and the money to pave streets in marble. What follows is that wealth, displayed downhill.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Site ticket around €40 in 2026, including the Experience Museum. Terrace Houses cost extra on top. Pay in lira or by card — euro cash is not accepted. Prices are revised regularly, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Summer roughly 08:00 to 19:00; night visits to 23:00 Wed–Sat in season. Winter hours are shorter. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Uneven ground from the start; the whole site is marble, gravel and steps. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Use the toilets at the upper gate — there are few inside, and the walk is two kilometres downhill from here.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk downhill through the gate and follow the marble street down for about a hundred and twenty metres. The small roofed theatre on your right, just past the State Agora, is the Odeon — our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Odeon (Council Hall)
stops.narration:
This little roofed theatre seated about fourteen hundred people, and it had two jobs. By day it was the bouleuterion — the council chamber where the city's ruling council of several hundred met to run Ephesus. By night it hosted concerts and poetry readings. The rows you see held the men who voted the budgets for the marble you are walking on.

It was built around 150 AD by a rich local named Vedius Antoninus, who paid for it the way rich Ephesians paid for everything public: out of his own pocket, with his name carved on it. That was the Roman system — the city gave the honour, the millionaire gave the building. The roof is long gone, but the semicircular rows and the stage wall give you the shape: small, steep, intimate, the opposite of the vast open theatre waiting at the bottom of the hill.

What you learn here is scale. Ephesus had a council chamber for its elite and, twenty minutes downhill, a theatre for twenty-five thousand ordinary people. Roman cities ran on both: the few deciding indoors, the many applauding outdoors. Keep both buildings in your head and the city's politics start to make sense.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Included in the site ticket. No separate fee.
stops.accessibility: Steep original steps between the rows; view it from the top rim if steps are a problem.
stops.insiderTip: Stand on the stage and speak at normal volume — even roofless, the curve throws your voice back at you.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue downhill past the State Agora for about two hundred metres to the narrow marble street dropping to the left. The gate with the Hercules relief, where the street squeezes through, is the start of Curetes Street — our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Curetes Street & Hercules Gate
stops.narration:
You are standing on the most beautiful street in Ephesus, and its name is a job title. The Curetes were the priests of Artemis — goddess of the hunt, patron of this city — and their names are carved on the columns lining this slope, because this street belonged to her cult the way a cathedral close belongs to its clergy.

Look at the gate first: two reliefs of Hercules, the club-carrying hero, strung across the street on pillars so close together that carts could not pass. That was the point. Wheeled traffic was barred and this became a pedestrian marble promenade — the Romans invented the car-free zone two thousand years early. Below the gate the street falls past fountains, baths and honorific statues, every surface marble, every base once carrying a bronze somebody.

The fact that reframes it: this street was repaved and re-statued for centuries, and the bases were reused shamelessly — an emperor fell from favour, his statue came down, and a new name went up on the old plinth. Read the doors and lintels as you descend: the stone is a palimpsest, each generation carving over the last. The ruts you can feel underfoot are the carts from before the gate went up.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Included in the site ticket. No separate fee.
stops.accessibility: Steep polished marble downhill — the slipperiest stretch on the walk when wet. Take it slowly.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the ancient advertisement carved into a slab near the bottom: a foot, a woman's head and a heart — a brothel sign pointing the way, two thousand years old.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk down Curetes Street for about a hundred and fifty metres, past the fountains and baths. The small exquisite temple with the arched Syrian gable, just before the street bends, is the Temple of Hadrian — our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: shankar s. from Dubai, united arab emirates, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Temple of Hadrian
stops.narration:
Small, perfect, and easy to miss if you are looking uphill at the crowds: this is the Temple of Hadrian, raised around 138 AD for the emperor Hadrian — the restless traveller-emperor who visited nearly every province and left buildings in most of them.

Read it from the top down. The Syrian gable — the arch rising out of a classical pediment — is the flourish that makes this little temple famous; architects still copy it. In the centre of the arch crouches Tyche, the goddess of a city's fortune, the luck of Ephesus carved in stone. Over the door, a Gorgon head bares its teeth to turn away evil — Medusa on guard duty. What you see is largely a 20th-century reassembly by Austrian archaeologists, but the pieces are original and the arch is the real shape.

The lesson is proportion. Ephesus had giant temples, and it had this jewel-box one, built by the city to flatter an emperor who liked to be flattered in architecture. Imperial cult — the worship of the emperor as a god — was the loyalty test of the Roman east, and this temple is where Ephesus passed it. The apostle Paul's riot started a few hundred metres downhill, when men who made silver Artemis shrines decided the new Christian preaching was bad for business. Same street, two religions, one economy.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Included in the site ticket. No separate fee.
stops.accessibility: Level marble forecourt; one step up to the temple. Fine from the street.
stops.insiderTip: Photograph it from slightly downhill and to the side — head-on it is always full of people, but the arch profile from an angle is empty and better.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn around: directly opposite the temple, across the street, is a covered entrance under a great protective canopy. That is the Terrace Houses — our next stop, and worth every cent of the extra ticket.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Kitkatcrazy, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Terrace Houses
stops.narration:
Pay the extra €15 and go in — this is the best-preserved Roman domestic interior anywhere outside Pompeii, and hardly anyone bothers. Seven houses of the Ephesian rich, built on terraces into the hill opposite the temple, lived in from the 1st century BC into late antiquity, and roofed today by a great canopy the Austrians raised over the whole block.

Walk them like an estate agent. Peristyle courtyards open to the sky, with fountains playing in the middle. Floors are mosaics — gods, muses, geometric borders so crisp they look laid last year. Walls carry frescoes in the deep reds and golds the rich loved. And underneath: hypocaust underfloor heating, hot air from a slave-stoked furnace circulating beneath suspended floors, plus piped running water and early toilets. The owners were the men who sat in the Odeon up the hill; this is where they went home to.

The fact to take with you: the houses were destroyed by earthquakes, not by war or Christians, and the rubble sealed them like a time capsule. Archaeologists found dinner still on the table, metaphorically speaking — the abandonment layer is that sudden. Give it forty-five minutes; the walkways are raised metal grids, mostly step-free, cool in the shade, and the finest mosaics are at the far end. Then come back out into the glare for the building everyone photographs.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Separate ticket around €15 on top of the site ticket in 2026. Verify at the gate — prices move.
stops.openingHours: Daily, roughly 09:00 to 17:00, and it closes earlier than the site (around 18:30 in the night-visit season). Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Raised metal walkways through most of the houses, largely step-free and shaded. The best option on the whole walk for anyone unsteady on marble.
stops.insiderTip: Walk all the way to the far end before looking properly — the finest peristyle and mosaics are deepest in, where the crowds thin out.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the canopy, turn downhill and walk about one hundred and fifty metres to the bottom of the slope. The great two-storey marble facade filling the square ahead is the Library of Celsus — our next stop, and the most photographed ruin in Turkey.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Rita1234, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Library of Celsus
stops.narration:
This facade is the most photographed ruin in Turkey, and it repays the attention. The Library of Celsus, finished around 135 AD, held some twelve thousand scrolls — the third-greatest library of the ancient world — and it is also a tomb.

The story first. Gaius Julius Celsus was governor of Asia, the province Ephesus capitalled. When he died, his son built this library in his honour for twenty-five thousand denarii, and buried his father in a sarcophagus in a vault beneath the reading room — a library as a headstone. The scrolls lived in niches in double walls, the air gap keeping the damp off the papyrus: Roman climate control. The four female statues in the niches are copies — Wisdom, Virtue, Thought and Knowledge — the originals are in Vienna, which tells its own story about where 19th-century finds went.

Then the ruin. Goths burned the interior in 262 AD; the facade stood another seven centuries until an earthquake dropped it. What you see is a 1970s Austrian anastylosis — fallen pieces reassembled, new stone only where the old was missing. Stand back across the square: the facade is deliberately wider at the base, a perspectival trick that makes it look taller than it is. The gate beside it opens to the commercial agora, the market square. And downhill, glinting at the end of Marble Street, is the theatre.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Included in the site ticket. No separate fee.
stops.accessibility: Level square in front, a few steps to the facade. The square itself is flat marble.
stops.insiderTip: Come back to the facade's optical trick: the columns lean inward and the base is wider than the top, so the building reads taller. Photograph it from the Marble Street side for the theatre-framed shot without the crowds.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk past the library down Marble Street for about three hundred metres, following the ruts. The enormous semicircle carved into the hillside ahead is the Great Theatre — our next stop. Enter and climb.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Benh LIEU SONG, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Great Theatre
stops.narration:
Climb. The Great Theatre seated some twenty-five thousand people — begun by the Greeks, rebuilt huge under the emperors Claudius and Nero — and from the top row the whole harbour plain opens below you. This was the largest theatre in Anatolia, and it was a working political machine, not decoration.

Two things happened here that explain the city. First, the entertainment: gladiatorial combats, wild-beast shows, civic assemblies that doubled as crowd control — bread and circuses with the emphasis on order. Second, the riot. Around 55 AD the apostle Paul preached here that gods made by hands are no gods at all, and Demetrius, a silversmith who made his living selling miniature silver Artemis shrines, led the craftsmen into this theatre shouting for two hours for great Artemis of the Ephesians. It is in the New Testament — the Book of Acts, chapter 19 — and you are standing where it happened.

Test the acoustics from the stage: a normal speaking voice reaches the top rows, no microphone, two thousand years of engineering in the curve. The theatre seats far fewer now — restoration and safety caps — and concerts still happen here under strict rules. Sit a minute. You have climbed from the council of the few to the assembly of the many, and the whole Roman social order is visible in the two buildings.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Included in the site ticket. No separate fee.
stops.accessibility: Steep original steps throughout; the climb is the point and it is demanding. View the stage from the orchestra floor if steps are a problem.
stops.insiderTip: Climb to the very top row: the harbour plain, the mountains and the theatre's sheer scale only read from up there — and the crowds rarely follow.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the theatre and walk west along the wide colonnaded boulevard stretching toward the distant plain. That is the Arcadian Way — our final stop, and the road to the sea that silted up.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Furkan Akkurt, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Arcadian Way & Harbour Gate
stops.narration:
This half-kilometre boulevard, colonnaded on both sides and once lit by street lamps, ran from the theatre to the harbour — and it is the reason Ephesus died. Walk it toward the empty plain and read the landscape: the sea is kilometres away now, but this road ended at quays.

The harbour was murdered by mud. The little Cayster river silted the bay relentlessly, and the Romans dredged heroically for centuries — emperors paid for harbour works the way modern states pay for motorways — but the mud kept coming. By late antiquity ships could not reach the quays, trade moved to ports that still floated, mosquitoes bred in the marshes, and the great city emptied toward the hill of Selçuk. The boulevard is named for the emperor Arcadius, who rebuilt it around 400 AD, near the end — fresh marble on a dying harbour.

So end here, at the lower gate, facing the plain that was the sea. Behind you: a council hall, a pedestrian shopping street, an emperor's temple, rich men's heated floors, a library-tomb for twelve thousand scrolls, and a theatre that once shouted down an apostle. Ahead: the museum in Selçuk, where the Artemis statues live, and the single standing column that marks the Temple of Artemis — Wonder of the World, now a marsh with storks. That contrast is Ephesus whole: what survives, what doesn't, and the mud that decided.

Catch the shuttle or walk the path back up to Selçuk from the lower gate. The museum closes later than the site and pairs perfectly with what you have just walked.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Included in the site ticket. The Selçuk museum (about €10) and St John's Basilica (about €6) are separate, in town.
stops.openingHours: Same hours as the site. The lower gate is also the night-visit entrance after 18:45 in season.
stops.accessibility: Long, mostly level boulevard — the easiest walking on the tour. Gravel and worn stone underfoot.
stops.insiderTip: Turn around at the far end and look back: theatre, library and hillside stacked in one view — the postcard shot with nobody in it, because everyone photographs the library alone.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Exit through the lower gate: shuttles, taxis and the path to Selçuk all leave from here. The Ephesus Museum in town (the Artemis statues) and the Basilica of St John on Ayasuluk Hill are the natural seconds — both are separate tickets.
